title: interactive-deployable-quickstart-kit
body:
Purpose:
This is a compact hands-on quickstart kit for a customer-facing workshop that demonstrates: (1) deploying a tiny edge proxy in front of Redwood Private/Dedicated endpoints for region-aware routing, (2) applying basic KV prefix caching to reduce token egress, and (3) running a simple canary rollout using the Console API. The artifact is intentionally lightweight so we can run the whole lab in 60–90 minutes with a small fleet (1-2 dev laptops + 1 cloud cluster).

High-level goals:
- Give customers a runnable reference they can adapt to on-prem or cloud.
- Surface the most common operational knobs (routing policy, cache TTL, batching window).
- Provide sample code and k8s manifests that are copy/paste ready.

Audience: solutions engineering workshop attendees (engineers, infra/platform owners), duration 60–90 min.

Prereqs (attendee):
- Laptop with kubectl and Docker installed
- Access to a small k8s cluster (min 2 vCPU node) or kind/local cluster
- Redwood API key or test sandbox credentials (we provide a temporary key in the workshop)
- Git client

Prep for instructor:
- Pre-create a short-lived API key and ensure Dedicated endpoint accessible from cluster IP ranges
- Have GitHub repo (linked above) forked and updated with the workshop branch
- Small slack channel for Q&A and a shared Confluence page for slides and follow-ups

Workshop flow (timed):
- 0–10m: Intro + architecture sketch (edge proxy, routing, cache, canary)
- 10–25m: Spin up cluster, deploy sample edge proxy service
- 25–50m: Wire proxy to Redwood endpoint, demonstrate cache and traffic shaping
- 50–70m: Run canary rollout and failure-injection test; collect metrics
- 70–90m: Wrap-up, Q&A, next steps

Reference architecture (short):
Edge proxy (stateless) -> routing policy -> Redwood endpoint (hosted/dedicated/private)
- Edge proxy holds short-lived KV cache for prefixes (per-customer key)
- Routing uses simple policy table (region -> preferred model variant -> fallback)
- Canary controlled via Console API or k8s labels

Quickstart commands (run in repo root):
1) clone repo and switch to workshop branch:
   git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/poc-edge-proxy.git
   cd poc-edge-proxy
   git checkout workshop/interactive-quickstart

2) build local docker image (optional for kind):
   docker build -t redwood/edge-proxy:local -f infra/Dockerfile .

3) deploy to cluster (k8s manifest in infra/k8s/):
   kubectl apply -f infra/k8s/namespace.yaml
   kubectl apply -f infra/k8s/edge-proxy-deployment.yaml
   kubectl apply -f infra/k8s/edge-proxy-service.yaml

Edge proxy minimal implementation (Python Flask adapter) - drop into src/app.py:
   from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
   import requests
   import os
   app = Flask(__name__)

   REDWOOD_ENDPOINT = os.environ.get('REDWOOD_ENDPOINT')
   API_KEY = os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY')
   PREFIX_CACHE = {}  # toy in-memory cache for demo only

   def call_redwood(payload):
       headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {API_KEY}', 'Content-Type': 'application/json'}
       r = requests.post(REDWOOD_ENDPOINT + '/v1/generate', json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=15)
       return r.json()

   @app.route('/generate', methods=['POST'])
   def generate():
       body = request.json or {}
       prefix = body.get('prefix')
       cache_key = prefix or 'default'
       if cache_key in PREFIX_CACHE:
           return jsonify({'from_cache': True, 'result': PREFIX_CACHE[cache_key]})
       # forward minimal payload to Redwood
       resp = call_redwood({'prompt': body.get('prompt', ''), 'max_tokens': 64})
       # store a tiny prefix cache (demo TTL not implemented)
       PREFIX_CACHE[cache_key] = resp.get('output')
       return jsonify({'from_cache': False, 'result': resp.get('output')})

   if __name__ == '__main__':
       app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=8080)

K8s manifest snippets (infra/k8s/edge-proxy-deployment.yaml):
   apiVersion: apps/v1
   kind: Deployment
   metadata:
     name: edge-proxy
     namespace: redwood-workshop
   spec:
     replicas: 2
     selector:
       matchLabels:
         app: edge-proxy
     template:
       metadata:
         labels:
           app: edge-proxy
       spec:
         containers:
         - name: edge-proxy
           image: redwood/edge-proxy:local
           env:
           - name: REDWOOD_ENDPOINT
             value: "https://dedicated.us-west-2.redwood.example.com"
           - name: REDWOOD_API_KEY
             valueFrom:
               secretKeyRef:
                 name: redwood-workshop-secrets
                 key: api_key
           ports:
           - containerPort: 8080

Note: manifests are intentionally simplified for clarity — in customer PoC we use secrets and nodeSelectors.

Canary rollout demo (k8s label switch + Console API):
- Have two versions (edge-proxy:v1 and edge-proxy:v2). We shift 10% traffic to v2 by updating service selector or using a simple traffic-split config in the Console.
- Instructor will run a script that toggles a k8s label and shows effect in tracing and latency dashboards.

Sample canary toggle script (scripts/canary-toggle.sh):
   #!/usr/bin/env bash
   set -e
   kubectl -n redwood-workshop label deployment edge-proxy canary=true --overwrite
   # optionally ping Console API to reflect in routing table
   curl -X POST $CONSOLE_API_URL/api/v1/rollouts -H "Authorization: Bearer $CONSOLE_API_KEY" -d '{"deployment":"edge-proxy","traffic":10}'

Observability: what to collect during the lab
- Request latency (p50/p95) at the proxy layer and between proxy -> Redwood
- Token consumption per request (to show cost savings from caching)
- Error rate and end-to-end success (HTTP 200 vs 5xx/4xx)
- Traces (sample traces) to show KV cache hits avoid a call to the model

Simple measurement exercise (5–10m):
- Before cache: run 30 requests, measure average token usage and latency
- After cache warmed: run same workload, compare tokens/tps and latency improvements
- Instructor leads a quick math: tokens saved * price per 1k tokens = estimated $/hr savings

Troubleshooting checklist (quick):
- Proxy 502s: check REDWOOD_ENDPOINT and API key scoping; test with curl to endpoint directly
- No cache hits: ensure prefix field is set in requests and proxy retains key (in demo TTL is unlimited)
- Canary not shifting traffic: verify service selector labels and confirm Deployment has v2 replica set
- High latency: check DNS/resolution, use kubectl exec to curl edge-proxy -> Redwood and capture latency

Classroom facilitation notes (tips for instructor):
- Keep the first run short — show the end-to-end with a single request, then expand into cache/canary deep dives
- Encourage attendees to edit the prefix cache strategy (e.g., LRU vs TTL) as a live exercise for 10–15m
- Use the slack channel for longer debugging; save time for one structured failure injection (simulate model OOM/fallover)

Post-workshop deliverables (for customer):
- Branch with completed sample code and manifests in the repo linked above
- One-pager with suggested production changes: TLS termination, mutual TLS to Redwood, k8s PodDisruptionBudget, HPA tuning, secrets via KMS
- Follow-up meeting to discuss Dedicated sizing and quantization options if they want lower cost per token

Notes to self / open questions to resolve before next run:
- Add a minimal redis-backed prefix cache (avoid in-memory) and test eviction semantics
- Add a small synthetic load generator in repo to produce steady-state qps for the canary step
- Confirm sample Console API call surface for customers without Console access (fallback: manifest-only canary demo)

Appendix: quick example curl to exercise proxy:
   curl -X POST http://<proxy-ip>/generate -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"prefix":"support:invoice","prompt":"Summarize the invoice notes: ..."}'

End of doc.
